full_judgment:
4. The learned Additional Assistant Judge having decreed the OC Suit No. 7 of 1992 on contest, the plaintiff-petitioner is now aggrieved by the impugned appellate judgment of reversal primarily on the ground that the lower appellate Court as the final Court of fact erred in law by reversing the judgment of the trial Court without discussing and considering the material evidence on record, thereby, being in violation of Order XLI, rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure (hereinafter referred to as the Code). The plaintiff-petitioner is also aggrieved by the fact that the lower appellate Court's judgment and decree occasions a failure of justice in view of its failure to advert to the reasons and material findings of the trial Court with regard to the evidence on record. This, the plaintiff-petitioner submits, has led to the lower appellate Court's assumption that there had been an entrustment of 51 decimals of land in Rafatullah Sarker as opposed to Rafatullah being an outright vendee of the said land. This further, as the plaintiff-petitioner submits, distracted the lower appellate Court from a proper consideration of the circumstances and overall scenario of fraud and collusion that pervades Rafatullah's actions thereby calling into question the genuineness and validity of the sale effected on 4-1-1986. 

 6. A consideration of the factual disparity between the cases as submitted by the parties at all stages of judicial consideration leading to this revision stage, leads this court to observe at the very outset that the case at hand is one that must necessarily be determined upon a preponderance and balance of evidence. That process necessarily entails a consideration of the rules of evidence in conjunction with those of pleading applicable in the facts and circumstances of this case. That exercise has further to be undertaken by focusing aptly and specifically on the issue as arises in this case. That issue specifically stated is one of cancellation of a duly registered sale deed being No. 413 dated 4-1-1986 on account of fraud and collusion. The impugned judgment reveals that the allegation of fraud and collusion has been generally made in the context of both the circumstances in which four deeds of sale pertaining to a total 51 decimals of land were executed and how, allegedly, in that process the sale deed-pertaining to the suit land came to be executed and registered unbeknown to the plaintiff-petitioner at the time of registration but subsequently revealed to him, and also by the fact that notwithstanding the execution and registration of such sale deed the defendant opposite party No. 5 is said never to have entered into possession of the suit land. Keeping in mind the grievance of the plaintiff petitioner that the impugned judgment is lacking in a proper and accurate consideration of all available evidence in this regard, especially in view of the fact that it is a judgment of reversal, this court at the very initial stage finds that the accurateness with which the lower appellate Court is to act in this regard has to be determined in light of established judicial authority which adhere to the view that as opposed to a detailed and exhaustive consideration of all reasons without fail, it will suffice if upon a clear reading of the impugned judgment it is evident that there has been a substantial consideration of the available evidence, albeit tampered with, and as held in Jatra Molum vs Pitambar reported in AIR 1915 Calcutta 99, "special reasons... for coming to an opposite conclusion," assigned by the lower appellate Court itself. Accordingly, as held in Abed Ali vs Sadek Ali reported in 9 DLR 128 and Abdul Azim vs Hashem Shaikh reported in 19 DLR 179 this would indeed, amount to a substantial compliance with Order XLI, rule 31 of the Code. Indeed, as expressed in Sashi Kumari Devi vs Dhirendra Kishore reported in AIR 1941 Calcutta 248 at page 251 it cannot readily be said "that a judgment of reversal is not a proper judgment merely because all the reasons given by the original court are not discussed. If the reasons given by the appellate Court are so cogent as to justify the finding, no discussion of other less convincing reasons seems to us necessary."
